summary: אִישׁ is a man: the male beside the woman who was taken from him (Gen 2:23), her husband, and a man as against God or beast. In the plural it names the men of a leader or a place, and joined to another noun it marks a person by his quality or calling (man of war, man of God). It is also scripture’s ordinary word for “each”, “one another”, “anyone” and, with a negative, “no one”, said even of animals and things. Its diminutive אִישׁוֹן, “little man”, is the pupil of the eye.

words.summary: The plural in ordinary use is אֲנָשִׁים, construct אַנְשֵׁי, the plural of the root אנש (אֱנוֹשׁ), which the text counts with אִישׁ; the plural of its own make, אִישִׁים, is found three times (Psa 141:4; Pro 8:4; Isa 53:3). The feminine beside it is אִשָּׁה (Gen 2:23), written under אנש.

senses.definition: A male human being, named beside the woman and set against her; a grown man as against a youth. Once of animals, the male with its mate.

evidence.note: “She shall be called אִשָּׁה, because מֵאִישׁ, from a man, this one was taken”: the first use of the word, and scripture’s own pairing of the two names.
מֵאִישׁ עַד־אִשָּׁה, “from man to woman”, beside child and infant, ox and sheep.
כָּל־אִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה, every man and woman whose heart moved them.
The man lying with the woman, and the woman.
A law for the male body.
“You are a youth (נַעַר), and he a man of war from his youth”: the grown man against the boy.
Eve at Cain’s birth: “I have gotten אִישׁ with Yahweh”, a man-child.
Of the animals entering the ark: seven and seven, אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, “a male and its mate”.
Gen 2:23 expounded: “man is not from woman, but woman from man”.

senses.definition: A woman’s man: her husband, usually with a suffix or the woman’s name (“her man”, “the man of Naomi”).

evidence.note: She gave also לְאִישָׁהּ עִמָּהּ, “to her man with her”.
“Your desire shall be to אִישֵׁךְ, and he shall rule over you.”
Leah: “now אִישִׁי will love me”.
“Elimelech, אִישׁ נָעֳמִי, died, and she was left, she and her two sons.”
“If she comes to belong to a man (תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ)”: if she marries.
הָאִישׁ הָאַחֲרוֹן, “the latter husband”, who took her to be his wife.
Of Israel restored: “you shall call me אִישִׁי, my man, and shall no longer call me בַּעְלִי, my owner (my Baal)”.
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife”; quoted in Mat 19:5 and Eph 5:31.

senses.gloss: man, as against God or beast
senses.definition: A human being as a kind: what God is not, and what the beasts are not. The messengers of God, appearing in a man’s form, are called by this word by those who see them.

evidence.note: לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב, “God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should change his mind”.
כִּי אֵל אָנֹכִי וְלֹא־אִישׁ, “for I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst”.
“For he is not a man as I am, that I should answer him.”
“God shall drive him away, not man.”
Assyria falls by “a sword not of man (לֹא־אִישׁ)”, parallel “not of אָדָם”.
לְמֵאִישׁ וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה, “from man to beast”.
“I am a worm and not a man.”
Rain on “a land of no man, a wilderness with no אָדָם in it”.
Abraham sees “three men (אֲנָשִׁים)”; two of them are “the two messengers” of Gen 19:1.
“A man wrestled with him until the dawn”; Hos 12:5 calls him a messenger (מַלְאָךְ).
“A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of a messenger of God”; verse 21 says he was the messenger of Yahweh.
הָאִישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵל, “the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision”.

senses.gloss: a man indeed: of courage, strength or standing
senses.definition: A man in the full sense, one who has a man’s strength and courage; and in the pairing with אָדָם, a man of standing beside the common man.

evidence.note: “Strengthen yourselves and be men (וִהְיוּ לַאֲנָשִׁים), Philistines … be men and fight.”
David to Solomon: “be strong, וְהָיִיתָ לְאִישׁ, and be a man”.
David to Abner: “Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel?”
“For as the man is, so is his strength (כָאִישׁ גְּבוּרָתוֹ).”
גַּם־בְּנֵי אָדָם גַּם־בְּנֵי־אִישׁ, “both sons of adam and sons of ish, rich and poor together”: the two halves answer in order to the poor and the rich.
“Sons of adam are a breath, sons of ish a lie”: low and high alike weigh nothing.
“אָדָם is bowed down and אִישׁ is brought low.”
“See if you can find a man, if there is one who does justice, who seeks faithfulness.”

senses.gloss: the men of a leader or place; a citizen, a follower
senses.definition: In the plural with a name, the men who belong to a leader (his followers, his fighting men), a house or a town (its inhabitants). The singular is used the same way as a collective: “the man of Israel” is the men of Israel, and is counted in thousands.

evidence.note: אַנְשֵׁי דָוִד, “the men of David”, his band.
“The men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from young to old, all the people.”
“None of the men of the house (מֵאַנְשֵׁי הַבַּיִת) was there in the house”: the household.
“All the man of Israel (כָּל־אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל) was gathered against the city as one man.”
The Gibeonites speak “to him and to the man of Israel”.
“The man of Israel was called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh.”
“And the man of Tob (אִישׁ טוֹב), twelve thousand men.”

senses.gloss: man of …: one marked by a quality, calling or people
senses.definition: Joined to a following noun, a person described by what he does, has or is given to (man of war, man of words, man of blood, man of pains); or set before a title or people-name with no added meaning of its own (a man, a priest; a man, an Egyptian).

evidence.note: יַהְוֶה אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה, “Yahweh is a man of war”: a warrior. The phrase says what he does, and is used here of God himself.
Esau “a man knowing hunting, a man of the field”; Jacob “a whole man, dwelling in tents”.
Noah, אִישׁ הָאֲדָמָה, “a man of the ground”.
“I am not a man of words (אִישׁ דְּבָרִים)”: not a speaker.
“Man of blood and man of worthlessness!”
אִישׁ מָוֶת אָתָּה, “you are a man of death”: one deserving it.
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת, “a man of pains and acquainted with sickness”.
“Daniel, אִישׁ־חֲמֻדוֹת, man greatly desired.”
אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי, “the man of my peace, in whom I trusted”.
אִישׁ עֲצָתוֹ, “the man of his counsel”: his counsellor.
“Moses, the man of God.”
אִישׁ מִצְרִי striking אִישׁ־עִבְרִי: “an Egyptian” and “a Hebrew”.
בַת אִישׁ כֹּהֵן, “the daughter of a priest”.
אִישׁ נָבִיא, “a prophet”.

senses.definition: Each one of a number, taken singly, with a plural verb or a suffix that picks up the single member; with “his brother” or “his fellow”, one another. Used of nations, animals and things as well as of men, so that the word here has become a pronoun. Doubled (אִישׁ אִישׁ, אִישׁ וָאִישׁ), any man whatever, every man.

evidence.note: “The two of them dreamed a dream, אִישׁ חֲלֹמוֹ, each his own dream, in one night.”
“They shall take for themselves, each man, a lamb for a fathers’ house.”
“Each man did what was right in his own eyes.”
The rest of the people he sent away, “each to his tent”.
The coastlands of the nations, אִישׁ לִלְשֹׁנוֹ, “each according to its tongue”: of peoples.
Of the divided carcasses: he set אִישׁ־בִּתְרוֹ לִקְרַאת רֵעֵהוּ, “each one’s half against its fellow”.
The cherubim, “their faces אִישׁ אֶל־אָחִיו, each toward its brother”.
“They said אִישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵהוּ, one to another.”
Abram and Lot “separated, אִישׁ מֵעַל אָחִיו, each from his brother”.
“They said each to his brother, What is it?”
אִישׁ אִישׁ מִבֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל, “any man of the house of Israel who …”.
אִישׁ אִישׁ … לֹא תִקְרְבוּ, “none of you shall approach …”.
“According to the pleasure of אִישׁ־וָאִישׁ, every man.”
“Of Zion it shall be said, אִישׁ וְאִישׁ, this man and that, was born in her.”
“You repay לְאִישׁ כְּמַעֲשֵׂהוּ, each according to his work”; taken up in Mat 16:27 and Rom 2:6.
“They shall no more teach, each his fellow and each his brother”; quoted in Heb 8:11.

senses.gloss: anyone, someone; (with a negative) no one
senses.definition: A person not specified: someone, anyone; with לֹא, אַל or אֵין, no one.

evidence.note: “If אִישׁ, anyone, can count the dust of the earth.”
אִישׁ אַל־יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנּוּ, “let no one leave any of it until morning”.
“No one shall come up with you, and let no one be seen in all the mountain.”
“None of us (אִישׁ מִמֶּנּוּ … לֹא) will withhold his tomb from you.”
“He saw that there was no one (כִּי אֵין אִישׁ).”
אֵין אִישׁ עִמָּנוּ, “no one is with us; see, God is witness”.
“Why, when I came, was there no one; when I called, none answering?”
“He saw that there was no one, and was appalled that there was none to intervene.”
וְלֹא נִמְלַט אִישׁ, “and not a man escaped”.

evidence.locator: Gen.2.23, מֵאִישׁ → ἀνδρός; Gen.3.16, אִישֵׁךְ → ἄνδρα; Hos.2.18, אִישִׁי → ἀνήρ; Psa.1.1; Zec.6.12; ἀνήρ renders אִישׁ ×1086

evidence.note: Gen 2:23 expounded: woman is ἐξ ἀνδρός, “from man”.
“The head of the woman is the man.”
“I betrothed you to one husband (ἑνὶ ἀνδρί)”: the husband sense.
“Jesus the Nazarene, a man (ἄνδρα) shown to you by God.”
God will judge the inhabited earth “by a man (ἐν ἀνδρί) whom he has appointed”.

evidence.locator: Gen.2.24, אִישׁ → ἄνθρωπος; Num.23.19, אִישׁ → ἄνθρωπος; Deu.33.1, אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים → ἄνθρωπος τοῦ θεοῦ; Isa.53.3; ἄνθρωπος renders אִישׁ ×452

evidence.note: Gen 2:24 quoted: “a man (ἄνθρωπος) shall leave his father and mother”; also Eph 5:31.
“O man of God”: the phrase אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים carried into the New Testament; also 2Ti 3:17.

evidence.locator: Jer.31.34 (LXX 38:34), אִישׁ … וְאִישׁ → ἕκαστος … ἕκαστος; Psa.62.13 (LXX 61:13), לְאִישׁ → ἑκάστῳ; ἕκαστος renders אִישׁ ×215

evidence.note: Jer 31:34 quoted: “they shall not teach each (ἕκαστος) his neighbour and each his brother”.
Psa 62:13 taken up: “he will repay each (ἑκάστῳ) according to his doing”.
“Who will repay each according to his works.”

parallels.note: אִישׁ in the first line is answered by אָדָם or בֶּן־אָדָם in the second. Where the two are set apart (Psa 49:3; 62:10) אִישׁ is the man of standing.

evidence.note: “The man of your right hand … the son of man you made strong for yourself.”
“To you, אִישִׁים, I call, and my voice is to the sons of adam.”

parallels.note: “A man”, as one of strength; the two stand in parallel lines.

evidence.note: “Write this אִישׁ childless, a גֶּבֶר who shall not prosper in his days.”
“They oppress a גֶּבֶר and his house, an אִישׁ and his inheritance.”

opposites.note: Woman, wife: the pair that makes up mankind, and a household.

evidence.note: “Man and woman, child and suckling.”

opposites.note: God, who is not a man.
A youth, not yet a man.

phrases.gloss: the man of God: a prophet, one who speaks for God

evidence.note: Moses.
Samuel: “a man of God is in this city … all that he says surely comes to pass.”
“You are a man of worth, and bring good news.”

phrases.gloss: one to another (a man to his fellow)

evidence.note: With אֶת: “each his fellow”.

phrases.gloss: one to another (a man to his brother)

evidence.note: Of the two cherubim.
With מֵעַל: “each from the other”.

phrases.gloss: as one man: all together, all at once

evidence.note: “The congregation was assembled as one man, from Dan to Beersheba.”
“If you kill this people as one man.”

phrases.gloss: sons of a man: men of standing
the man of Israel: the men of Israel as a body
men of the name: men of renown

evidence.note: “The mighty men who were of old, the men of the name.”

phrases.gloss: the man of the space between (two armies): a champion

evidence.note: Goliath, who came out from the camps of the Philistines.

words.gloss: pupil of the eye; the dark middle (of night)
words.summary: אִישׁ with the ending ‑וֹן: “little man”, the small figure of himself a person sees in another’s eye, and so the pupil. Psa 17:8 sets it beside בַּת־עַיִן, “daughter of the eye”, a name of the same kind, and Arabic names the pupil “the man of the eye”. It has few uses (four, with a fifth as the written text of Pro 20:20) and no cognate of its own form, so its tie to אִישׁ rests on the form, the parallel names and the fit of the sense. In Pro 7:9 and 20:20 it is the black centre of the night or of darkness, as the pupil is the black centre of the eye.

senses.definition: The pupil, the centre of the eye: the part a person guards before all else, and so a figure for what is kept with the greatest care.

evidence.note: Yahweh found Jacob in a wilderness land: “he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him כְּאִישׁוֹן עֵינוֹ, as the pupil of his eye”.
“Keep me כְּאִישׁוֹן בַּת־עָיִן, as the little man, the daughter of the eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings.”
“Keep my commandments and live, and my teaching as the pupil of your eyes.”
The companion name alone: “let not בַּת־עֵינֵךְ, the daughter of your eye, be still”.
The same figure with another word: “he who touches you touches בָּבַת עֵינוֹ”.

senses.definition: The blackest part of the night or of darkness: its pupil.

evidence.note: “In the twilight, in the evening of the day, בְּאִישׁוֹן לַיְלָה וַאֲפֵלָה, in the pupil of night and thick darkness”: the last and darkest of the four.
“His lamp shall be put out in the pupil of darkness”: written בְּאִישׁוֹן חֹשֶׁךְ, read בֶּאֱשׁוּן.

evidence.locator: Deu.32.10, כְּאִישׁוֹן עֵינוֹ → ὡς κόραν ὀφθαλμοῦ; Psa.17.8 (LXX 16:8), כְּאִישׁוֹן → ὡς κόραν; not used in the New Testament

parallels.note: “Daughter of the eye”: the pupil named as a small person, set in apposition to אִישׁוֹן.
Thick darkness, beside “the pupil of night”.

phrases.gloss: as the pupil of the eye: with the closest care

cognates.gloss: man; male; citizen or native of a place; member of a group
cognates.note: The same word in the nearest language to Hebrew, with the same spread: a man (“bad men, bandits”, KAI 26 A 13/14), a male set against ʾšt “female” (kl ʾdm ʾm ʾš ʾm ʾšt, “every person, whether male or female”, CIS i 5511.6), the man of a place (ʾš kty, “a man of Kition”; ʾš knʿn, “a man of Canaan”) and the member of a body (ʾš mḥnt, “a man of the army”, a soldier), as Hebrew says אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל and אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר. Phoenician writing does not tell š from ṯ, so it does not show the older sound.

evidence.locator: pp. 75–76, ʾŠ I, pl. ʾŠM (1. MAN; 2. MALE; 3. CITIZEN, RESIDENT, NATIVE of a specific place; 4. MEMBER(S) of a group; 5. pl. STAFF of a bureau)

cognates.note: The phrase אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים in Phoenician, on a seal: “Baalyaton, the man of the god, of Milqart of Tyre”. Phoenician also has ʾš ʾdr, “great man”, as a title of a king (p. 80).

evidence.locator: p. 81, ʾŠ ʾLM (‘MAN OF THE GOD’ = PROPHET); p. 80, ʾŠ ʾDR I (‘GREAT MAN’ = KING)

cognates.note: On the stele of Mesha: ואש גד ישב בארץ עטרת מעלם, “and the man of Gad had dwelt in the land of Ataroth from of old”: the collective singular with a people’s name, exactly as אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Jdg 20:11) and אִישׁ טוֹב (2Sa 10:6).

cognates.gloss: man; husband; “a man to his brother” = one another (Sabaean)
cognates.note: Sabaean has the word with the y written (ʾys) and without (ʾs), in three of the Hebrew uses: a man (“he killed two men”), a husband (“for the safety of her husband”), and the reciprocal idiom (ʾysm bʿbr ʾḫhw, “they sent to one another, lit. a man to his brother”), which is אִישׁ אֶל־אָחִיו. Its s is the sibilant that answers to Hebrew שׁ as š. Sabaean keeps ʾns “man” beside it as a separate word, as Hebrew keeps אֱנוֹשׁ beside אִישׁ.

evidence.locator: p. 14, ʾYS I, n. ʾs, ʾys ((1) MAN; pejoratively, FELLOW; (2) HUSBAND; (3) in ʾys nbt, FAMILY HEAD (?)) (J612/12; C308/17; A788/3)

cognates.gloss: mankind; a human being, a man; “the man of the eye” = the image seen in the black of the eye, the pupil
cognates.note: Arabic has no ʾ‑y‑s “man”; its word is of the root ʾ‑n‑s, the root of אֱנוֹשׁ and of the plural אֲנָשִׁים. Whether אִישׁ is that root with the n lost, or a root of its own, is not settled by the evidence (see the entry’s note), so this is recorded as possible only. It is kept for the phrase إِنْسَانُ العَيْنِ, “the man of the eye”, Arabic’s name for the pupil and for the image reflected in it: an independent witness to the figure behind אִישׁוֹן.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 113, إِنْسٌ (n1336): mankind, the opposite of jinn; p. 114, إِنْسِىٌّ (n1340): a human being, a man
Book I, p. 115, إِنْسَانٌ (n1344): إِنْسَانُ العَيْنِ, the image that is seen reflected in the black of the eye; or the pupil of the eye

doctrine.statement: Balaam is given to say, “God is not a man (אִישׁ), that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should change his mind: has he said, and will he not do it?” (Num 23:19). Yahweh says the same of himself: “I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst” (Hos 11:9). Job knows that he cannot answer God as an equal, “for he is not a man as I am” (Job 9:32), and Elihu sets the two against each other, “God … not man” (Job 32:13). Scripture therefore uses אִישׁ and אֵל as opposites: what God is, a man is not. When the song at the sea says “Yahweh is a man of war” (Exo 15:3) it is the idiom “man of …” for one who does a thing, a warrior, and says what he did to Pharaoh’s host, not what he is.

The prophets call the one who was to come אִישׁ: “a man of pains and acquainted with sickness” (Isa 53:3), and “Behold, a man, Branch is his name … he shall build the temple of Yahweh” (Zec 6:12). The apostles speak in the same way after his resurrection: Peter preaches “Jesus the Nazarene, a man shown to you by God by mighty works … which God did through him” (Act 2:22), Paul that God “will judge the inhabited earth in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Act 17:31), and that “there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Since God is not a man (Num 23:19), and Jesus is called a man before and after he was raised, and is set beside the one God as the mediator between him and men, Jesus is not God but the man whom God raised up, worked through and appointed.

Abraham “lifted up his eyes and saw three men (אֲנָשִׁים) standing by him” (Gen 18:2); “the men” go on toward Sodom (Gen 18:22), and the two who arrive are “the two messengers” (Gen 19:1), still called “the men” as they bring Lot out (Gen 19:10, 16). “A man” wrestled with Jacob (Gen 32:25), and Hosea says “he strove with the messenger and prevailed” (Hos 12:5). Manoah’s wife says “a man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of a messenger of God” (Jdg 13:6), and only afterward did Manoah know “that he was the messenger of Yahweh” (Jdg 13:21). Daniel speaks of “the man Gabriel” (Dan 9:21). So the messengers of God come in the form of men and are not at first told apart from them, which is why the New Testament says that some “received messengers without knowing it” (Heb 13:2).

The woman was taken out of the man and named from him: “she shall be called אִשָּׁה, because from אִישׁ this one was taken”, and “therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Gen 2:23–24). Jesus quotes the verse and draws the conclusion, “so they are no longer two but one flesh; what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Mat 19:5–6); Paul reasons from the order of the making, “man is not from woman, but woman from man” (1Co 11:8), and applies the “one flesh” to Christ and the ecclesia (Eph 5:31). The husband’s name is the plain word “her man”, and Yahweh takes it for himself in the day he restores Israel: “you shall call me אִישִׁי, my man, and shall no longer call me בַּעְלִי, my owner” (Hos 2:18). Paul uses the same figure: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you a pure virgin to Christ” (2Co 11:2).

The law forbids putting fathers to death for sons or sons for fathers: “each (אִישׁ) shall be put to death for his own sin” (Deu 24:16). Jeremiah says the same of the days to come, “each shall die for his own iniquity” (Jer 31:30), and the psalm of God, “you repay each according to his work” (Psa 62:13). The distributive אִישׁ carries the point: the reckoning is with each person singly. Jesus says of his coming in the glory of his Father, “then he will repay each according to his doing” (Mat 16:27), and Paul, that God “will repay each according to his works” (Rom 2:6).

“Surely as a shadow a man (אִישׁ) walks about; surely for a breath they are in turmoil; he heaps up, and does not know who will gather” (Psa 39:7). “Sons of adam are a breath, sons of ish a lie; in the balances they go up, together lighter than a breath” (Psa 62:10): the man of standing weighs no more than the common man. And no man can buy another out of death: “a brother no man can by any means redeem, nor give to God his ransom” (Psa 49:8), though both “sons of adam and sons of ish, rich and poor together” are called to hear it (Psa 49:3). Man of every rank is passing and cannot deliver himself or his brother from death; the redemption has to come from God.

note: Root: איש is the key the words are filed under and is kept; no other entry has it. No verb of the root occurs (הִתְאֹשָׁשׁוּ, Isa 46:8, sometimes read “show yourselves men”, is filed under אשש and not taken). Whether אִישׁ is a root of its own or the root אנש with the n lost is open. For a separate root: the long i written with י and kept before suffixes (אִישִׁי, אִישָׁהּ), the rare plural אִישִׁים, Phoenician ʾš / Moabite אש with no n, and Sabaean, which has both ʾys and ʾns as separate words. For one root: the working plural אֲנָשִׁים, the feminine אִשָּׁה, and the absence of ʾyš “man” from Arabic, Aramaic and Akkadian. The entry takes it as its own key and records Arabic ʾins as possible only. Gen 2:23 pairs אִישׁ and אִשָּׁה as one name and its feminine; that verse is scripture’s own account and is cited as such, whatever the older consonants were (אִשָּׁה and אֱנוֹשׁ are in the entry for אנש, id enosh, and are not words here). Tokens: a.da.ab counts the plural אֲנָשִׁים / אַנְשֵׁי with אִישׁ, so the sense ish-men-of rests largely on plural forms; if the enosh entry claims those tokens the count here should be looked at. Left out: אַךְ “surely, only” (a.da.ak), which is under this key only by the alphabet and has its own entry (ak, root אכ); אִיתַי (a.da.ah, 0 tokens), a cross-reference to אֵת; the names אִישׁ־בֹּשֶׁת, אֶשְׁבַּעַל and אִישְׁהוֹד, which have name entries. אֱשׁוּן (a.gd.ae, 0 tokens) is the read form at Pro 20:20 where the written text has אישון; it is given to אִישׁוֹן. A derivation of אֱשׁוּן from Akkadian isinnu “fixed time, festival” has been proposed and was not followed: the written text and Pro 7:9 give “pupil of darkness / of night”. No Aramaic word: scripture’s Aramaic and the Peshitta use גְּבַר / ܓܒܪܐ and אֱנָשׁ / ܐܢܫ, which belong to other entries; the Peshitta renders אִישׁ “each” by ܐܢܫ (Heb 8:11; Mat 16:27). Sounds: only Sabaean (s¹) and, as possible, Arabic (s) show the sound behind ש, and both show š; Ugaritic iṯ “there is” (the name iṯbʿl beside Punic ʾšbʿl, Krahmalkov p. 81) belongs with יֵשׁ / אִשׁ “there is”, not with אִישׁ. Leads not followed: Old Aramaic ʾyš “man, each” (CAL; the inscriptions of Sefire and Carpentras), not verified in a source here; the Siloam inscription’s אש אל רעו (Hebrew, not a cognate); any link between אִישׁ and יֵשׁ / אִשׁ (2Sa 14:19; Mic 6:10); Akkadian has no cognate noun. Psalms and other books are cited by Hebrew verse numbers (Hos 2:18; Zec 2:12; Num 30:7). Krahmalkov and Biella were checked against the page images, not only the OCR.
